amendments.rule: Expect more fusion rather than new rules: *Nor* for waw plus a negative, *But* for `כִּי אִם`, *whatsoever* for `כֹּל אֲשֶׁר`. The same *Nor* may rest on a present negative in one line and a gapped one in the next; align what is actually there. **Distance does not break these fusions.** Where the ASV's single word still says what every morpheme in it says, the unit stands however far apart they stand: `וְ ... לֹא` → *Nor* across a fronted prepositional phrase or object, `לֹא ... לְעוֹלָם` → *never* across the verb it negates. This is the far side of rule 30's contiguity condition, and the difference is what the English word carries. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* drops the preposition's own sense, so rule 2 splits it and the preposition is `unrepresented`; *Nor* still carries both the coordination and the negation and *never* both the negation and the time, so nothing is left over to mark. Head a *Nor* on the negative, which is what distinguishes it from a bare *and*. A *never* is a genuine tie between the negative and the temporal noun — the corpus heads it both ways — so choose, and say in the note which reading you took and that the corpus heads it both ways. **A *cannot* is not one of these fusions, because the verb's lexeme stands outside it.** Where the ASV writes *cannot* for a negated verb, the word carries the negation together with a modal English has supplied, and it goes whole to the negative while the verb keeps its subject pronoun and its lexical verb under rule 17: `לֹא יִצְעָדוּ` → *they* ***cannot*** *go* gives *cannot* to `לֹא` and *they go* to the verb, exactly as rule 48 gives such a word to the privative `מִן` that carries the negation there. The corpus aligns `לֹא` alone to *cannot*, headed on it, in fourteen units. **But where `יָכֹל` stands in the clause, that verb is what the modal renders**, and the two morphemes share the one indivisible word — `לֹא אוּכַל` → *I cannot*, `לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *they cannot*, `לֹא נוּכַל` → *we cannot* — headed on *cannot*, which is how the corpus reads all eleven of those units. And where the ASV writes the negation and the modal as two words instead — *are not able*, *shall not be able* — nothing is indivisible, rule 2 splits them, the negative takes only its own *not*, and the rest belongs to the verb, its complement headed by rule 44. Read the English the ASV wrote and the verb the Hebrew wrote, not the modality the Hebrew implies.
amendments.why: Rule 35 is where the contract decides which morpheme a single English negative word belongs to and heads on, and JER.10.5 met the member it had not considered: *cannot*, twice, for a negated imperfect with no verb of ability in the clause. The principle was already in the contract but scoped to one construction — rule 48 gives such a *cannot* to the privative `מִן` because that is what carries the negation there — so a pass meeting a plain `לֹא` had nothing to read, and could hand the modal to the verb or make the two share a unit. Both halves are read off the corpus rather than imposed: LEMMA=לֹא shows fourteen single-token units aligned to *cannot* headed on it (1KI.3.8, 1KI.18.12 among them), and every one of the eleven units where the word is shared writes a `יָכֹל` form beside it (GEN.19.19, GEN.19.22, GEN.34.14, GEN.44.22, GEN.44.26, GEN.24.50, GEN.29.8, 1SA.17.39, ISA.56.10, JER.6.10), so the carve-out is what keeps the new sentence from contradicting them. The two-word case is stated so that JER.10.10's 'are not able to abide' for `לֹא` plus `כּוּל` is not swept in by the surface resemblance of `יָכִלוּ` to `יָכֹל`.

conventions: מֵאֵין כָּמוֹךָ (vv. 6, 7): the ASV's 'There is none like unto thee' spends nothing on the מִן, so it is its own unrepresented unit under rule 40, while אַיִן carries the presentative dummy and the copula and heads on 'none' under rule 50, and כְּמוֹ takes 'like unto' headed on 'like' (rule 24). BSB represents the מִן in both verses; that is the documented convention difference and not a correction.

'cannot' (v5, twice) is one English word fusing the negation with a modal English supplies for the imperfect, and it goes whole to לֹא while the verb keeps its subject pronoun and lexical verb ('they' + 'go'), as rule 48 already gives such a word to the privative מִן that carries the negation there. No verb of ability stands in either clause. Where the ASV instead writes the negation and the modal as separate words — v10's 'are not able to abide' for לֹא יָכִלוּ, whose verb is כּוּל and not יָכֹל — rule 2 splits them, לֹא takes only 'not', and the rest is the verb's under rule 44. The difference is read off the English the ASV wrote, not off the Hebrew's modality.

report: Checked every multi-treatment bucket in the 48-lemma table. Each one is the ASV rendering a morpheme differently in a different English context, which the source licenses: waw to and / But / but / yea / that (v4's 'that' opens the result clause the ASV wrote); מִן to from / out of / at / by / of / unrepresented; כִּי to For / for / because / that / 'forasmuch as'; לְ to to / unto / for / of / When / unrepresented; אֵת to unrepresented, 'of' (v21 'inquired of'), 'in' (v5); לֹא to not / no / cannot; and the הוּא suffixes to possessive, object and — in vv. 9, 13, 18 — subject pronouns under rules 18 and 40. No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference.

Read the dump end to end for the added-versus-folded boundary the table cannot see. The six added units (v8 'but', v9 'which', v14 'and', v14 'his', v18 'it', v19 'my') are each a word no morpheme in its clause licenses; every supplied word folded into a unit elsewhere (v5 'a', the supplied 'the's, v9 and v13 'there is', v17 'O thou that', v23 'that walketh') is licensed by a morpheme or by rules 15, 20, 36, 41, 46, 49. The one pair that looks like a split and is not: v9's 'which' is added because the Hebrew writes the antecedent and the ASV subordinates a finite clause to it (rule 46's last paragraph, rule 55), while v23's 'that' stays with הֹלֵךְ because that is an articleless attributive participle (rule 41). The contract separates them and the chapter followed it.

Article accounting was checked chain by chain against rule 29's counting (vv. 2, 3, 7, 9, 13, 16, 18, 22, 23). v2 holds both patterns in one verse and gets both right: דֶּרֶךְ הַגּוֹיִם is rendered arthrously at the rectum, so the article takes the 'the' standing before its own word and the construct a supplied one, while אֹתוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם is rendered anarthrously, so the article's single 'the' is fronted. v16 ('the former of all things') and v23 ('the way of man') are the same fronting case; v18's two articles in בַּפַּעַם הַזֹּאת are both unrepresented because the demonstrative morpheme licenses the only determiner written (rule 41's 'only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner').

Copula and presentative placement is uniform across the chapter: nominal anchor in vv. 9, 13; prepositional predicate in vv. 5, 14, 16, 19, 23 (rules 20, 49); existential אַיִן in vv. 5, 6, 7, 20, always headed on the negation word and never on 'there' (rule 50), with the referential subject pronoun going to the suffix in v20. Rule 44's split between a phrasal particle (head on the verb: vv. 12, 13, 17, 18, 25) and a complement (head on the complement: vv. 5, 10, 13, 14, 24, 25) is applied the same way throughout.

BSB: all eight disagreements are convention differences, none an error. The four R cases are rule 40 recastings the ASV leaves nothing for — אֶל before a bare object (v2), the מִן of מֵאֵין (vv. 6, 7), and לָהֶם after 'distress them' (v18). v3's suffix on כְּרָתוֹ has no English because the ASV writes the fronted 'a tree' as the object. v5's גַם is unrepresented because the ASV writes no 'also'; the waw and אַיִן already carry all of 'neither', and folding גַם in would make that word say something it does not say. v18's הַ and v23's וְ are words the ASV simply does not write. I changed no accepted edge.
Two conventions recorded (מֵאֵין, and the 'cannot' reading) and one amendment proposed to rule 35 for the fused negation-plus-modal 'cannot'. No patches: the chapter is internally consistent.
